## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\caption{The five-level machine stack within the governance envelope.}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why is a robot that has operated for weeks without a single crash not evidence that the machine is safe?_

Weeks of incident-free operation establish behavior solely under encountered benign conditions; they provide no empirical evidence that the machine can survive edge-case anomalies. In classical software engineering, executing millions of requests without an exception implies code stability. In physical AI, that intuition collapses: zero code exceptions does not equal zero hazard. An unperturbed neural foundation policy can execute bit-exact instructions with zero memory faults, yet command catastrophic motor torque because of an out-of-distribution optical flow pattern or retroreflective floor surface. Software in physical AI effectively "wears out" through environmental distribution shift rather than mechanical fatigue. Waiting for rare corner cases in passive operation is unviable: a tenfold rarer event requires ten times the operating exposure to witness, and encountering it during deployment risks catastrophic physical damage.

Whole-system verification transforms safety assumptions into systematic, repeatable fault injection experiments executed across simulation, processor-in-the-loop testbenches, and physical dynamometers. Each experiment challenges timing, data freshness, and kinetic authority boundaries, verifying whether the machine detects faults and enforces safe fallbacks within declared budgets. Within the governance envelope, rigorous verification binds the Brain's cognitive models, the Nervous System's deterministic monitors, and the Body's physical dynamics into empirical evidence capable of justifying, restricting, or denying deployment.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Physical failure modes and measurement limits providing verification targets originate in @sec-body-measuring-limits.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Define an operating envelope and derive its pass conditions from the machine's stopping budget
- Derive a fault list from design records and forward physical analysis, including authority and compound faults
- Evaluate which simulation and hardware tests support each claim and where their evidence ends across the four-stage qualification ladder
- Bound physical tail risk using Extreme Value Theory (EVT) and validate sim-to-real transfer discrepancies
- Apply zero-miss sizing to a declared, weighted fault population and state what it leaves uncovered
- Design fault-injection tests that challenge timing, data validity, and authority claims on physical hardware
- Construct the Verification Matrix contract record, maintaining failed, invalid, and unobservable trials distinct from passes

:::

## Operational Survival Versus Formal Safety Evidence {#sec-verification-fault-injection}

An incident-free operating log answers only the conditions it encountered. It does not exercise a frozen camera frame, a brownout, or a bus occupied by direct memory access (DMA) traffic. Relying on accumulated road exposure is the **Million-Mile Fallacy**\index{Million-Mile Fallacy}: assuming that accumulating millions of incident-free road miles (or billions of simulated frames) empirically proves that an autonomous robot is safe for deployment. Because benign miles overwhelmingly sample the high-probability center of the operational envelope, passive road testing leaves safety-critical boundary conditions unexplored. Waiting for those conditions is slow, because a tenfold rarer event takes on average ten times the exposure to observe (the exposure wall of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits), and on a machine it is also unsafe, because when the event finally occurs in operation it arrives as motion that no software action can recall. Whole-system verification therefore turns each safety claim into a deliberate fault, injected under containment and scored against a test oracle and limits declared before the run. The claims come from the records the earlier chapters produced, ending with the authority record of @sec-intervention-authority-log, which names who may command each actuator channel and what must happen when a handover goes unanswered.

To understand how these verification trials feed into operational release, it helps to conceptualize a **safety case**\index{Safety case!legal brief model} as a structured legal brief presented to a regulatory authority or release auditor. In systems engineering, safety assurance arguments are formalized through the **Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE)**\index{Claim-Argument-Evidence!assurance framework} framework and visualized via **Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)**\index{Goal Structuring Notation!safety assurance}:

- **Claims (Goals)**: Explicit, falsifiable assertions about the system's runtime properties (for example, "The mobile manipulator operates collision-free along warehouse aisles under declared lighting and floor conditions").
- **Arguments (Strategies)**: Logical rationales explaining *why* the claims are valid, decomposing complex goals into verifiable sub-claims (such as "Argument by control barrier certificate invariance," "Argument by dual-channel sensor plausibility," and "Argument by fault-injection falsification").
- **Evidence (Solutions)**: Objective, reproducible empirical exhibits that ground each argument (such as oscilloscope traces of power-rail droop, hardware-in-the-loop test manifests, and microsecond-timestamped fieldbus logs).

This structured assurance framework forms the backbone of modern safety standards:

1. **ISO 26262 ASIL (Automotive Safety Integrity Level)**\index{ISO 26262!ASIL ratings}: The automotive functional safety standard evaluates hazardous operational events across three orthogonal risk dimensions: **Severity** ($S0\text{--}S3$, potential physical harm to humans), **Exposure** ($E0\text{--}E4$, operational likelihood of encountering the driving scenario), and **Controllability** ($C0\text{--}C3$, ability of a human driver or bystander to prevent injury). The cross-product of these dimensions yields four integrity grades, ranging from **ASIL A** (lowest severity/exposure) to **ASIL D** (highest criticality, such as unintended full steering or acceleration at highway speeds). Achieving ASIL D demands rigorous architectural defenses: dual-core lockstep microcontrollers, hardware Single-Point Fault Metrics (SPFM) exceeding $99\,\text{percent}$, Latent Fault Metrics (LFM) exceeding $90\,\text{percent}$, and random hardware failure rates bounded below $\lambda \le 10^{-8}\,\text{failures/hour}$ ($10\text{ FIT}$, or Failures In Time per billion operating hours).
2. **ANSI/UL 4600 (Evaluation of Autonomous Products)**\index{ANSI/UL 4600!autonomous safety standard}: While ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 provide prescriptive rules for electrical and electronic hardware faults, they explicitly assume that the software algorithm's specification is complete and correct. For physical AI systems driven by deep neural networks and foundation models, that assumption collapses. A vision-language-action policy can execute without a single bit flip, memory fault, or code exception, yet misclassify an obstacle due to distribution shift. ANSI/UL 4600 addresses this gap: it is a **goal-based, autonomous safety standard** that requires developers to present a comprehensive GSN safety case proving *why* the autonomous machine is safe. It mandates evidence covering non-deterministic machine learning behaviors, operational design domain (ODD) boundary escapes, sensor fusion degradation, and unexpected human interactions.

A safety case does not rely on subjective assertions; every high-level claim must link directly to empirical exhibits.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-rack-end-oracle
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RACK-END FAULT-INJECTION ORACLE FOR THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: fault-injection scene, operating envelope, fault list, oracles,
# │          hardware injection, fault manifest, fallacies, and summary.
# │ Goal: Derive the two oracle bounds (brake onset after the last valid renewal,
# │       stopping distance at the aisle speed) and the envelope points that
# │       F1-F4 and A1-A4 are injected at, all from the machine's registry entry.
# │ Show: 82 ms onset bound; 997.4 mm budget and 102.6 mm spare at 1.3 m/s;
# │       78.9 ms of travel in that spare, 174.7 ms at the 1.2 m/s takeover
# │       speed; the 1.39 m/s dry and 1.09 m/s inspected-floor ceilings; the
# │       17.3 V control-rail sag; the permission rail's 2.0 s hold-up against
# │       1497.35 ms from flag to brakes set (F4b); F1's stop oracle from the
# │       last valid renewal (780.4 mm at 1.3 m/s); the F1 record's oracle at
# │       the restricted 1.0 m/s point (759.3 mm from the last valid renewal);
# │       the Class 3 tank contrast (volume, not distance); F2's refusal
# │       threshold, the 51.6 ms budgeted age plus the 0.2 ms clock-conversion
# │       bound (51.8 ms upper age).
# │ How: calc_safe_stopping_distance and calc_max_permitted_velocity with the
# │      C² suffix (a_eff = a_brake / 1.5) and the three fixed overheads;
# │      calc_voltage_droop for the rail; tank arithmetic by conservation of volume.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, kilogram, microsecond, millisecond, second, meter, millimeter
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_max_permitted_velocity,
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
)
from mlsysim.physics import calc_voltage_droop
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_voltage,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_temperature,
    fmt_mass,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RackEndVerification:
    """Oracle bounds and envelope points for fault injection at the rack end."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (clock-conversion bound, @sec-perception-observation-contract)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    heartbeat_timeout = AISLE.heartbeat_timeout  # category: chosen
    enforcer_deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_takeover = AISLE.t_takeover_in_loop  # category: illustrative
    v_takeover = AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    mu_dry = AISLE.mu_dry  # category: illustrative
    mu_insp = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative
    payload = RM.onboard_payload_capacity  # category: chosen
    rail_nominal = RM.control_rail_nominal  # category: chosen
    rail_low = RM.control_rail_battery_low  # category: illustrative
    rail_r = RM.control_rail_resistance  # category: illustrative
    rail_dropout = RM.control_rail_dropout  # category: illustrative
    i_rail = AISLE.i_rail_transient  # category: illustrative
    rail_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen
    brake_engage_max = RM.spring_brake_engage_max  # category: illustrative
    g = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # physical constant (defined); category: derived
    # Scenario assumptions local to this chapter
    ambient_lo = ureg.Quantity(5.0, ureg.degC)  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    ambient_hi = ureg.Quantity(35.0, ureg.degC)  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    lease_probe = 5 * millisecond  # proposal injected after expiry; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    v_restricted = (
        1.0 * meter / second
    )  # restricted-mode aisle speed on inspected floors, below the inspected-floor ceiling; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    late_onset = 30 * millisecond  # example late brake onset (STL margin); scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    queue_delay = 100 * millisecond  # unbudgeted ISP-to-backbone queue (fallacy); scenario assumption; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    a_eff = (a_brake / 1.5).to(meter / second**2)
    onset_bound = (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    upper_age = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # F2: refusal threshold on the evidence's upper age
    lease_probe_at = (t_lease + lease_probe).to(millisecond)
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    budget = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_aisle, tau_delay, a_eff, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    c2 = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_aisle, a_brake)
    c2_distance = c2["distance"].to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    t_spare = (spare / v_aisle).to(millisecond)
    per_ms = (v_aisle * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    budget_takeover = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_takeover, tau_delay, a_eff, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track).to(
        millimeter
    )
    spare_takeover = (d_clear - budget_takeover).to(millimeter)
    t_spare_takeover = (spare_takeover / v_takeover).to(millisecond)
    ceiling_dry = calc_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, tau_delay, a_eff, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track).to(
        meter / second
    )
    mu_min = float((a_brake / g).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    a_insp = min(a_brake, (mu_insp * g).to(meter / second**2))
    budget_insp = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_aisle, tau_delay, a_insp / 1.5, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track).to(
        millimeter
    )
    ceiling_insp = calc_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, tau_delay, a_insp / 1.5, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track).to(
        meter / second
    )
    rail_sag = calc_voltage_droop(i_rail, rail_r).to(ureg.volt)
    rail_min = (rail_low - rail_sag).to(ureg.volt)
    # F4: from the undervoltage or feed-loss flag, stop onset, the longest resident
    # stop inside the envelope (inspected floor at its ceiling), and brakes set
    flag_onset = (t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    stop_insp_ceiling = calc_c2_stop_suffix(ceiling_insp, a_insp)["duration"].to(millisecond)
    flag_to_set = (flag_onset + stop_insp_ceiling + brake_engage_max).to(millisecond)
    holdup_margin = (rail_holdup - flag_to_set).to(millisecond)
    # F1 record at the restricted point, scored from the last valid renewal
    f1_preonset = (v_restricted * onset_bound).to(millimeter)
    f1_c2 = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_restricted, a_insp)["distance"].to(millimeter)
    f1_stop_bound = (f1_preonset + f1_c2 + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    # F1 at the aisle speed, scored from the same event (last valid renewal)
    f1_aisle_stop_bound = (v_aisle * onset_bound + c2_distance + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    budget_restricted = calc_safe_stopping_distance(
        v_restricted, tau_delay, a_insp / 1.5, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(millimeter)
    late_extra = (v_aisle * late_onset).to(millimeter)
    stop_late = (budget + late_extra).to(millimeter)
    rho_late = (budget - stop_late).to(millimeter)
    queue_extra = (v_aisle * queue_delay).to(millimeter)
    queue_breach = (queue_extra - spare).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(onset_bound.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: brake onset 82 ms after the last valid renewal.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 5e-3, "Canon: tau_delay 133.6 ms.")
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 5e-3, "Canon: t_age 51.6 ms.")
    check(abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, "Clock-conversion bound must match the perception contract's 0.2 ms.")
    check(abs(upper_age.magnitude - 51.8) < 5e-3, "Canon (D22): F2 refuses above a 51.8 ms upper age.")
    check(abs(budget.magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, "Canon: budget at 1.3 m/s is 997.43 mm.")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, "Canon: spare at 1.3 m/s is 102.57 mm.")
    check(abs(c2_distance.magnitude - 633.75) < 5e-3, "Canon: C2 stop at 1.3 m/s is 633.75 mm.")
    check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 78.9) < 5e-2, "Canon: T_latest 78.9 ms.")
    check(abs(ceiling_dry.magnitude - 1.3898) < 5e-5, "Canon: dry-floor ceiling 1.3898 m/s.")
    check(abs(ceiling_insp.magnitude - 1.0947) < 5e-5, "Canon: inspected-floor ceiling 1.0947 m/s.")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Canon: friction needed for a_brake is 0.204.")
    check(abs(rail_min.magnitude - 17.3) < 5e-3, "Canon: control rail sags to 17.3 V.")
    check(rail_min < rail_dropout, "The sagged rail must fall below the regulator dropout for F4.")
    check(v_aisle < ceiling_dry and ceiling_insp < v_aisle, "Aisle speed sits between the two ceilings.")
    check(budget_insp > d_clear, "At the aisle speed the inspected-floor budget must exceed the clear distance.")
    check(mu_insp < mu_min < mu_dry, "Dry floor supports a_brake; the inspected floor does not.")
    check(queue_extra > spare, "The unbudgeted queue must exhaust the spare.")
    check(abs(overhead.magnitude - 190.0) < 1e-6, "Canon: fixed overhead 190 mm.")
    check(rho_late.magnitude < 0, "A late onset must drive the distance margin negative.")
    check(abs(v_takeover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.2) < 1e-9, "Canon: in-loop takeover speed 1.2 m/s.")
    check(t_spare_takeover >= t_takeover, "At the slowed speed the spare must cover the in-loop takeover.")
    check(t_spare < t_takeover, "At the aisle speed the spare cannot cover the in-loop takeover.")
    check(abs(spare_takeover.magnitude - 209.7) < 5e-2, "Canon: spare at the 1.2 m/s takeover speed is 209.7 mm.")
    check(abs(t_spare_takeover.magnitude - 174.7) < 5e-2, "Canon: T_latest 174.7 ms at 1.2 m/s.")
    check(abs(flag_onset.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: stop onset within 22 ms of the flag.")
    check(abs(rail_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: permission-rail hold-up 2.0 s.")
    check(abs(flag_to_set.magnitude - 1497.35) < 5e-3, "Canon: flag to brakes set 1497.35 ms.")
    check(abs(holdup_margin.magnitude - 502.65) < 5e-3, "Canon: hold-up margin 502.65 ms.")
    check(v_restricted < ceiling_insp, "The restricted point must sit below the inspected-floor ceiling.")
    check(abs(f1_preonset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-6, "Canon: 82 mm of pre-onset travel at 1.0 m/s.")
    check(abs(f1_c2.magnitude - 637.3) < 5e-2, "Canon: C2 stop at 1.0 m/s on the inspected floor is 637.3 mm.")
    check(abs(f1_stop_bound.magnitude - 759.3) < 5e-2, "Canon: F1 stop oracle 759.3 mm from the last valid renewal.")
    check(
        abs(f1_aisle_stop_bound.magnitude - 780.35) < 5e-3 and f1_aisle_stop_bound < budget,
        "F1 stop oracle at 1.3 m/s is 780.35 mm from the last valid renewal.",
    )
    check(
        abs(budget_restricted.magnitude - 960.9) < 5e-2 and budget_restricted < d_clear,
        "Canon: budget at 1.0 m/s on the inspected floor is 960.9 mm.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=None)
    a_insp_str = fmt_acceleration(a_insp, precision=2)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    upper_age_str = fmt_latency(upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=None)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=None)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    onset_bound_str = fmt_latency(onset_bound, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    lease_probe_at_str = fmt_latency(lease_probe_at, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    heartbeat_timeout_str = fmt_latency(heartbeat_timeout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    enforcer_deadline_str = fmt_latency(enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_takeover_str = fmt_latency(t_takeover, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_takeover_str = fmt_velocity(v_takeover, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(t_spare, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    spare_takeover_str = fmt_length(spare_takeover, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_takeover_str = fmt_latency(t_spare_takeover, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    per_ms_str = fmt_length(per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    ceiling_dry_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_dry, precision=2)
    ceiling_insp_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_insp, precision=2)
    budget_insp_str = fmt_length(budget_insp, unit=meter, precision=2)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_insp_str = fmt(mu_insp, precision=2)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(payload, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    ambient_lo_str = fmt_temperature(ambient_lo, precision=0)
    ambient_hi_str = fmt_temperature(ambient_hi, precision=0)
    rail_nominal_str = fmt_voltage(rail_nominal, precision=None)
    rail_low_str = fmt_voltage(rail_low, precision=1)
    rail_dropout_str = fmt_voltage(rail_dropout, precision=None)
    i_rail_str = fmt_current(i_rail, precision=0)
    rail_min_str = fmt_voltage(rail_min, precision=1)
    flag_onset_str = fmt_latency(flag_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    rail_holdup_str = fmt_latency(rail_holdup, unit=second, precision=None)
    flag_to_set_str = fmt_latency(flag_to_set, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, precision=None)
    f1_stop_bound_str = fmt_length(f1_stop_bound, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    f1_aisle_stop_bound_str = fmt_length(f1_aisle_stop_bound, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    budget_restricted_str = fmt_length(budget_restricted, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    late_onset_str = fmt_latency(late_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    late_extra_str = fmt_length(late_extra, unit=millimeter, precision=None)
    stop_late_str = fmt_length(stop_late, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    queue_delay_str = fmt_latency(queue_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    queue_extra_str = fmt_length(queue_extra, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    queue_breach_str = fmt_length(queue_breach, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

Consider the warehouse mobile manipulator running its aisle at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) toward a rack end where a person may step out. Weeks of clean runs at that speed say little about four faults the design claims to contain: a proposer that renews its lease and then stalls (F1), an observation that reaches the permission path with a stale or corrupt capture time (F2), a burst of lost EtherCAT frames between the permission path and the drives (F3), and a sag of the `{python} RackEndVerification.rail_nominal_str` control rail when an inference burst coincides with the drive motors (F4). These failure modes comprise the eight core physical and authority benchmarks evaluated throughout this chapter: physical faults F1–F4 and authority transfer faults A1–A4 (formalized in @tbl-15-fault-classification). None of them shows in an operating log, because each leaves the machine running normally until the moment a stop is needed. The lease catches a stall, the evidence-epoch check a stale capture time, the drive's fieldbus watchdog a lost frame, and the permission path's undervoltage monitor, on its own held-up rail, a sag of the shared one. Each fault is injected at the rack end, together with the four authority faults that @sec-intervention-authority-log hands over (A1–A4), and every stopping trial is scored against the onset and distance bounds that @sec-verification-operating-envelope derives from the stopping budget.

An injected fault turns a physical run into a test result that can support a safety case only when the run satisfies the five requirements of the **cyber-physical test contract**:

1. **A bounded claim:** stating the exact invariant the machine must maintain (for the base at the rack end, a stop that ends inside the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clear distance);
2. **Defined test conditions:** specifying the initial speed, payload, floor friction, ambient temperature, and supply-voltage range;
3. **A precommitted oracle\index{Testing!Oracle}:** an automated evaluator that inspects recorded telemetry against the claim without human intervention or post-hoc adjustments;
4. **A stated sampling and injection procedure:** deliberately driving the machine toward its performance limits and injecting faults into sensors, buses, and actuators; and
5. **Provenance\index{Provenance}:** the complete metadata record of model weights, calibration tables, sensor serial numbers, and raw bus logs permitting independent reproduction.

The base's stopping claim and the arm's latch-force claim require separate envelopes, injection points, and pass conditions; this chapter follows the stopping claim. The first decision is where nominal regulation must yield to an independent containment response.

## The Operating Envelope {#sec-verification-operating-envelope}

The **operating envelope**\index{Operating envelope!definition} is the target ODD (@sec-evaluation-what-measured) extended inward to the machine's own conditions: compute load, supply voltage, bus jitter, thermal state, and operator response time. The sets nest: the ODD contains the declared ODD, which contains the target ODD, and the operating envelope pairs the target ODD with the machine's internal conditions. Defining this envelope requires precise numerical boundaries for an automated test framework to drive the system deterministically across each constraint. For the mobile manipulator, the envelope is a set of declared points rather than one nominal condition: the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed; payloads of zero and the `{python} RackEndVerification.payload_str` rack capacity; floor friction of at least `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_min_str`, the value the `{python} RackEndVerification.a_brake_str` credible deceleration needs, on dry aisles, and of at least `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` on floors under the site's inspection regime; and ambient temperatures from `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_lo_str` to `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_hi_str`. For inspected floors the envelope declares a restricted point at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str`, the speed of the restricted configuration that the enforcement record declares valid down to that friction (@sec-enforcement-telemetry), and trials there use a test floor whose measured friction sits at the `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` qualification value, so that the stop they exercise is the one friction bounds.

Each point is paired with the machine's internal conditions: application-processor load up to its peak inference burst, the control rail anywhere from its `{python} RackEndVerification.rail_low_str` battery-low point to its `{python} RackEndVerification.rail_nominal_str` nominal, EtherCAT jitter, and the safety microcontroller's thermal state. One further point is the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_takeover_str` to which the machine slows before it requests a remote assistant's in-loop takeover, and only that point carries the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_takeover_str` takeover time (@sec-intervention-authority-transitions).

An operating envelope is distinct from the larger **survival envelope**\index{Survival envelope!definition} that encloses it. Inside the operating envelope the learned policy and the tracking controllers regulate the process. When a disturbance, a sensor failure, or a compute stall pushes the machine across that boundary, nominal regulation is conceded, and the objective becomes bringing the body to a bounded, safe state before structural limits are breached. For the mobile manipulator, the survival envelope is the broader region of speed, floor friction, and machine state within which the fallback ladder's stop rung, and its inhibit rung as the last resort (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder), can still bring the base to rest short of the rack end and keep the arm's contact force below its limit. Beyond it lies structural failure, where stored energy exceeds what the hardware can dissipate.

Defining the boundary of the operating envelope requires deriving limits from first principles rather than asserting convenient software timeouts. At the rack end the limit is the stopping budget. Stopping distance grows linearly with the pre-brake delay and quadratically with speed (@eq-body-stopping-distance), and the finished budget of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget), with its `{python} RackEndVerification.tau_delay_str` pre-brake delay, the smooth resident stop that @sec-planning-behavior-seam commits to, and the tracking inset, sets a ceiling of `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_dry_str` on a dry floor. At the chosen `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` the machine needs `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` of the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clear distance and keeps `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` in reserve, a distance it covers in `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`.

Two oracle bounds follow, and every stopping trial in this chapter is scored against both. Brake onset must come no later than `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` after the last valid renewal, the lease path of @sec-nervous-cadences: the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str` lease, one `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` tick of the permission loop, one `{python} RackEndVerification.t_bus_str` bus cycle, and `{python} RackEndVerification.t_act_str` of brake onset. The rail faults of F4 take their onset from the undervoltage flag instead. The stop, measured by instruments independent of the machine, must end within the distance allowed from the same event the fault is referenced to. For a fault that follows a target's appearance, that distance is the `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` the budget allows. A stalled proposer offers no target appearance, so its stop, like its onset, is measured from the last valid renewal, and the travel during the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` before brake onset, the resident stop, and the tracking inset give `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` at the aisle speed.

Neither bound depends on the proposer. A chunk policy that stalls cannot delay brake onset, because the stop begins when the lease expires rather than when the proposer notices, so a test of F1 measures the permission path and not the policy. The budget protects a static obstacle at the clear distance, and a trial against a static target says nothing about a person still walking toward the machine, a premise the site's crossing rule carries (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion).

On the mobile manipulator, separate minimum and maximum values for individual variables fall prey to the **Curse of 1D Scalar Sweeps**: failing to capture the true operating boundary because physical and computational dimensions are coupled along a multi-dimensional state-space manifold. The `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed and an inspected floor with friction `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` each lie inside their declared ranges, yet together they fall outside the envelope. On that floor friction, not the brake, sets the credible deceleration, which drops to `{python} RackEndVerification.a_insp_str`. The resident stop lengthens, and the budget at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` grows to `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_insp_str`, past the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clear distance; the speed boundary on that floor is `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str`, which is why the envelope's restricted point sits below it. Payload couples less visibly. It enters no term of the budget, but the credible deceleration was declared for the loaded machine, so a campaign run only unloaded never tests the value the budget rests on. The true operating boundary is a surface in state, parameter, and latency space, and a valid verification suite must probe that combined surface rather than isolated scalar limits.

A boundary stays honest only if every parameter carries its unit, its provenance, its calibrated uncertainty, and an engineer accountable for it. A credible deceleration of `{python} RackEndVerification.a_brake_str` is incomplete until the record says whether it came from stopping trials at the loaded mass, a drive datasheet, or a friction model, and with what resolution the external distance reference measured each stop. A new wheel tread compound or new EtherCAT slave firmware obliges that owner to re-evaluate whether the boundary has moved.

Testing the envelope means attacking its boundary surface. Interior points, where the base crawls unloaded across a dry floor on fresh camera frames, show only that the machine works under ideal conditions. The test framework places points on, just inside, and just outside each consequential boundary. Points just inside check that the policy keeps closed-loop stability\index{Closed-loop stability} under the largest permitted stress; points on the boundary check that margins survive nominal sensor noise; points just outside check that the enforcer takes authority from the policy predictably and halts the base within the survival envelope before the clear distance is gone.

Probing this boundary surface formalizes the critical distinction between classical **Functional Safety** (governed by ISO 26262 and IEC 61508) and the **Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF)**\index{Safety of the Intended Functionality!ISO 21448}\index{SOTIF!ISO 21448}\index{Functional safety!vs. SOTIF} (governed by ISO 21448). Classical functional safety frameworks assume that operational hazards arise from *system faults*: broken wiring harnesses, electrical shorts, bit flips in memory, or software syntax bugs. If every hardware and software component operates strictly according to its engineering specification, classical functional safety considers the system non-hazardous. In physical AI systems, this premise fails. A vision transformer or learned depth estimator can execute with zero memory faults, zero numerical exceptions, and bit-exact instruction execution, yet fail to detect an obstacle due to unmodeled sunlight glare, retroreflective surfaces, or novel semantic objects outside its training distribution. This hazard arises from **functional insufficiency**—a fundamental performance limitation of learned perception in open environments, occurring in the total absence of an electrical or software fault. Verification of the operating envelope under SOTIF requires systematically identifying these unknown-unsafe conditions through adversarial boundary search, mapping the envelope within which perception is statistically valid, and demonstrating that the deterministic enforcer catches functional insufficiencies before physical clearance is breached. Yet while SOTIF verifies that the system responds safely to sensory ambiguity in the world, the enforcer's ultimate ability to arrest physical momentum still rests on the deterministic integrity of the underlying hardware under electrical and mechanical stress.

::: {#psp-verification-hardware-falsification .callout-perspective title="The hardware falsification principle"}
If a safety property cannot be deterministically falsified by injecting a physical or electrical fault\index{Fault injection!hardware} on target hardware, the property is an unverified assumption rather than an engineering invariant.
:::

Once every constraint, latency budget, and environmental limit is stated as a number, the design claims of the preceding chapters become targets for fault injection\index{Fault injection}, each with a threshold that must trigger protective intervention\index{Protective intervention}.

## Deriving the Fault List {#sec-verification-deriving-fault-list}

Fault derivation bridges the gap between high-level architectural claims and falsifiable physical test vectors. Rather than relying on generic fault taxonomies, the verification suite derives fault cases from two complementary directions: inverting the formal design claims of preceding chapters, and working forward from physical and tribological mechanics.

### Inverting design records and the five-element chain {#sec-verification-inverting-records}

The first source of faults is the design records, inverted. @Sec-data through @sec-evaluation state the learned policy's properties: its training distribution, its state-action assumptions, and its inference latency ceilings. @Sec-perception through @sec-placement state interface and execution properties such as bus allocations, observation freshness, and estimation bounds, and @sec-intervention states how quickly authority can leave a failing policy and who holds the override. If the machine's records state that the chunk policy renews its proposal every `{python} RackEndVerification.chunk_period_str` at every speed up to the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_drive_str` drive limit, the verification suite inverts that claim by injecting stalled renewals, delayed observations, and out-of-range encoder readings to test whether the permission path detects the violation within its budget.

For a single fault, the bounded claim and the injection procedure of that list become a five-element chain comprising the negated condition, the physical injection point, the expected detector, the bounded response, and an observable pass condition, and a recorded design property becomes a testable fault only when all five are defined. For F2, the navigation camera stamps each frame at capture, and the frame's age at dispatch is budgeted at `{python} RackEndVerification.t_age_str` (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration). Converting that stamp to the safety microcontroller's clock adds the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_sync_str` bound of the observation contract (@sec-perception-observation-contract), so the permission path refuses evidence whose upper age exceeds `{python} RackEndVerification.upper_age_str`. The negated property holds a frame at the image signal processor while preserving its capture stamp, so that it arrives past that threshold. The expected detector is the permission path's check of each proposal's evidence epoch, the required response is refusal of any proposal built on that evidence followed by the resident stop, and the observable pass condition is the pair of oracle bounds, brake onset within `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` of the last valid renewal and a measured stop within `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str`. When any element of this chain cannot be defined or observed, the system contains a **verification gap**\index{Verification gap!definition}. A verification gap indicates that the claim cannot be falsified by test. Such gaps cannot be ignored; they require dedicated hardware instrumentation, a narrower operational claim, or a redesign of the execution path.

Inversion also reaches the learned proposer's assumptions, because distribution shift is a system fault even when every frame arrives intact. A chunk policy trained in simulation on dry concrete with friction `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_dry_str` proposes decelerations that a floor at `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` turns into wheel slip. Inverting that evaluation claim means injecting the unmodeled traction. Sensor bias and data perturbations are injected for the same reason, because a policy with a high nominal reward can still command jittering actuators once its inputs are perturbed. The machine then fails on valid, uncorrupted commands, because software and mechanics stay coupled across the causal boundary (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary).

At each inter-module contract, the fault list negates the property at its physical point of handoff: observation freshness, state validity, intent lifetime, planning deadlines, enforcement independence, and resource allocation. For the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str` chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences, the test environment injects an otherwise valid proposal `{python} RackEndVerification.lease_probe_at_str` after its last renewal and confirms that the permission path rejects it as expired. For the enforcer's claimed independence from the policy computer, the test saturates the shared memory bus with DMA traffic and confirms that the enforcer still meets its `{python} RackEndVerification.enforcer_deadline_str` deadline inside each `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` tick. The discipline cuts both ways. Bus starvation, clock skew, and supply fluctuation are injected where the design claims tolerance, because a fault drawn from a generic menu invents a requirement the machine was never specified to meet.

Inversion has a structural limit. It produces only the faults the design team already modeled, so the list is only as complete as the design claims. If no record says how the base's spring-applied brake behaves when its lining glazes after repeated stops, there is nothing to invert, and the failure never reaches the suite.

### Forward physical analysis and common-cause modes {#sec-verification-forward-analysis}

A second, independent source works forward from the physical machine, enumerating what the body, the power network, the floor, and the environment can do regardless of what the software believes. Wheels skid when a commanded deceleration exceeds what the floor can transmit; brake linings glaze under repeated stops; tires wear and change the rolling radius that odometry assumes; drive vibration loosens a camera mount until its calibration drifts. These hazards originate in mechanics and tribology, outside every abstraction the software reasons over. Leveson's **Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP)**\index{Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes!definition} framework[^fn-std-stpa-leveson] [@leveson2011engineering] brings them into hazard analysis.

For example, start with the physical hazard of a base that keeps driving after the permission path has commanded a stop at the rack end. The unsafe control action is continued drive torque after the stop command. The test injects a welded drive-enable contactor or a stuck brake-release solenoid on the test aisle, observes wheel speed and brake current independently of the commanded stop bit, and requires the permission path to remove drive power through its second channel, safe torque off. The precommitted pass condition is a measured stop within `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` across the declared speed, payload, and floor-friction points; an unmeasured wheel speed makes the trial unobservable for the braking claim. This forward chain yields an injection and oracle even if the original software requirements omitted a welded contactor.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_fault_injection_coverage_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder showing fault injection climbing from SRAM bit-flips up to physical dyno shaft jamming."}

*Fault injection climbs from software bit-flips to physical dyno shaft jamming.*
:::

[^fn-std-stpa-leveson]: **STAMP/STPA Hazard Analysis**\index{Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis!emergent hazards}: Developed at MIT by Nancy Leveson, STAMP treats safety as a control problem rather than a component-reliability problem, so hazards appear as unsafe control actions at interfaces, such as a seam where bus latency or filter lag erodes a stability margin. STPA is the hazard-analysis method built on it.

Working forward exposes fault classes that no software record implies: clock loss, brownouts that leave logic levels between valid thresholds, drive-switching interference coupling into encoder lines, corrupted configuration memory, and reset lines that bridge domains meant to be independent. If the safety microcontroller and the application processor shared one power-management IC, an undervoltage transient during an inference burst could reset the microcontroller at the moment the proposer loses control. No software record contains that failure, because each module assumes its supply is ideal. This establishes the **Isolated Permission Rail Invariant**: an enforcer cannot arrest a failing policy if it shares the power rail that browns out during the policy's compute surge. The safety runtime must outlive the faulted workload it supervises, powered from an isolated, held-up auxiliary supply.

Forward analysis also tests the common-cause independence claims of @sec-nervous and @sec-placement. Two paths isolated on a diagram often share one physical vulnerability, as when the lidar and a redundant bumper switch are routed through one cable carrier, share an analog reference inside one converter, or are built on timer silicon with the same errata. A transient that latches up both channels at once defeats any argument that treats their failures as independent. **Common-cause analysis**\index{Common-cause analysis!definition} traces routing, power paths, and clock trees so that no single physical event can disable both the policy and the intervention mechanism.

The physical source extends to operator error and foreseeable misuse (@sec-intervention). Floor staff jumper a rack-end presence sensor during maintenance, park a pallet jack across a marked crossing, or unplug a warning beacon to silence it, while remote assistants request speeds the aisle does not allow. When a remote assistant commands the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_drive_str` drive limit in the aisle, the verification framework must verify that the command is denied by capability, or clamped under a `manual_drive` entry to the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, and that the permission check runs on it like any other proposal.

Working forward from the physical machine adds one representative mechanical class, the actuator jam, to the record-derived list in @tbl-15-fault-classification. Completeness still requires a separate hazard-analysis argument for the specified plant and operating envelope.

### Transduction-layer cyber-physical attacks {#sec-verification-transduction-attacks}

Working forward from physical transducers also requires testing against **transduction-layer cyber-physical attacks**\index{Cyber-physical security!transduction attacks}\index{Sensor spoofing!physical injection}\index{Cybersecurity engineering!ISO/SAE 21434}. In connected autonomous systems, physical AI introduces attack surfaces that bypass traditional network firewall abstractions by exploiting the physics of sensory transduction. Resonant acoustic injection (targeting the micro-mechanical proof masses of MEMS gyroscopes with ultrasonic frequencies) can induce false angular rates in inertial navigation without corrupting a single bus packet. Similarly, optical laser injection and rolling-shutter illumination strobes can saturate camera photodiodes to blind range estimators, while adversarial physical patches (high-contrast geometric patterns placed on warehouse walls or floor surfaces) can exploit the gradient landscape of neural perception backbones to cause false negative obstacle detections. Under **ISO/SAE 21434 (Road vehicles — Cybersecurity engineering)**, these threats are co-engineered alongside functional safety faults: a cyber-physical intrusion is evaluated by its ability to cross the causal boundary into hazardous actuation. The verification suite must confirm that the enforcer's cross-sensor plausibility checks (such as comparing wheel odometry against optical flow, or checking camera evidence epochs against IMU integration bounds) detect transduction anomalies and engage the fallback ladder before false perceptual claims can command torque.

Besides inverted claims and forward hazards, the fault list must test the authority cases A1–A4 of @sec-intervention-authority-log, each a row of @tbl-15-fault-classification, tested with the machine in the state that makes intervention urgent, the loaded base approaching the rack end. The handover deadline is tested at both speeds where @sec-intervention-authority-transitions sets it. Once the machine has slowed to `{python} RackEndVerification.v_takeover_str` for an in-loop request, the `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_takeover_str` reserve gives an unacknowledged handover `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_takeover_str` to fall back; at the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, for a handover the policy requests without slowing, the reserve's travel time shrinks to `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`. A handover tested with the base parked tests none of the deadlines that matter.
